blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Distinguish production from productivity, calculate labour productivity, and explain why the difference matters to a firm.

blocks.heading: Two measures of output
blocks.text: Production is the total quantity of goods or services a firm makes in a period: Kaoko Juice of Oshakati produced 6 000 bottles last month. Productivity is output per unit of a factor of production over the same period - most often output per worker. Production counts the bottles; productivity asks how much each worker, or each machine, produced. A Vietnamese shoe factory and a Namibian one can be compared on this common scale even when their total outputs differ.

blocks.heading: Calculating labour productivity
blocks.text: Labour productivity = total output / number of workers. Kaoko Juice made 6 000 bottles with 15 workers, so productivity was 6 000 / 15 = 400 bottles per worker. If the same 15 workers produce 7 500 bottles after a training course, productivity becomes 7 500 / 15 = 500 bottles per worker, a rise of 500 - 400 = 100 bottles per worker. The same arithmetic works for any factor: bottles per machine, loaves per oven.

blocks.heading: Why firms watch productivity
blocks.text: Cost per unit depends on how much each worker produces. Where productivity rises, the same wage bill covers more bottles, so cost per bottle tends to fall; the firm can cut its price, or hold the price and earn more on each sale. A fall in productivity works in reverse: the same wages are spread over fewer bottles, and cost per bottle rises. Productivity, not production, is what tells a firm whether its workforce is turning effort into output well.

blocks.heading: Production is not productivity
blocks.text: Learners often treat the two as one idea. Production is a total; productivity is a rate per factor. The test: two laundries each washing 9 000 loads a month are equal in production, but if one uses 12 workers and the other 18, the first washes 750 loads per worker and the second 500, so the first is the more productive. A firm can even raise production while productivity falls - taking on extra workers whose added output is smaller per worker than before - so a growing total is not on its own a sign of efficiency.

blocks.heading: What raises production, and what raises productivity
blocks.text: Production and productivity respond to different influences. Production depends on how many factors the firm employs - workers, machines, land and materials - on how productive they are, and on demand for the product, because a firm tends to produce what it expects to sell. Kaoko Juice could raise production from 6 000 to 8 000 bottles a month by hiring 5 more workers: if each new worker produces as much as the others, 20 x 400 = 8 000 bottles, but productivity stays at 400 bottles per worker. Productivity rises only when each worker, or each machine, produces more. Its main influences are education and training, which build skill and cut mistakes; more and better capital and technology, such as a faster bottling machine; motivation, through pay, conditions and recognition; management and organisation, such as dividing the work into tasks and arranging the line well; and the quality of inputs, from sound fruit to workers' health. In South Korea, decades of heavy spending on schooling and modern equipment are widely credited with raising output per worker. Training at Kaoko Juice raised output from 400 to 500 bottles per worker with the same 15 workers: production and productivity rose together.
